item.title: Understanding Brian Flores’ Blitz-Heavy Scheme
item.description: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Eric Wilson #55 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates with Blake Cashman #51 against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings under defensive coordinator Brian Flores run a unique scheme that has become a hot topic around the league after dominating every opponent en route to a 6-0 start for the Vikings. It is a blitz-heavy scheme but it’s not about simply dialing up pressure and hoping not to get burned. It’s Not Just About Rushing the Passer The first thing to know about Flores’ blitz-heavy scheme is it’s not just about rushing the passer, it’s a total defensive philosophy designed to stop the run and pass, dictate the terms of engagement, and make execution for the offense more difficult- forcing mistakes. There are several intertwined elements to what is really a unique scheme in the NFL at the moment, which is rare. Foundational Elements and Principles The foundation of Brian Flores’ scheme is a five (or more) man front paired with a secondary playing zone coverage. That is what you are likely to see on around 80% of the Vikings’ defensive plays. A 5+ Man Attacking Front The defensive front operates an attacking, aggressive style, with defensive linemen penetrating gaps and linebackers blitzing and twisting. This contrasts with other schemes where defensive linemen are tasked with defending a gap-and-a-half or two gaps by catching blocks or taking on double-teams to keep linebackers clean. Edge rushers are tasked with setting edges, rushing the passer, or dropping into coverage. Beyond that, Flores will often place or walk-up other defenders to the line of scrimmage, either bringing or simulating additional pressure. The key in all of this is to pressure the quarterback and offense both physically and mentally- and not just occasionally but every down. Zone Coverage On the back end, the Vikings play a variety of zone coverages, frequently disguised pre-snap, and also man coverage on rare occasions. This contrasts with the man coverage that has typically accompanied blitzing fronts in the past. One key here is that the zone shell coverage is better able to prevent or limit the explosive plays that can result when a blitz doesn’t get home in time. The other key is that the coverages vary and can be difficult (or impossible) for a quarterback to differentiate pre-snap and often early post-snap as well. Numbers, Angles, Matchups- and Chaos The object of every football play or scheme is to create advantages in numbers (players), angles, and/or matchups. Brian Flores’ scheme is no different in that regard. item.title: Wisconsin's Adaline Sheplee has efficient performance in exhibition win | Takeaways
item.description: MADISON – Eight was enough for the Wisconsin women’s basketball team Oct. 28. The Badgers scored a 101-69 victory over Wisconsin -Eau Claire in their only exhibition of the preseason with just eight players due to injuries and Illness. All eight Badgers played at least 20 minutes. Six scored in double figures and six had at least two assists. Freshman Adaline Sheplee scored 25 points on 8-for-10 shooting. Iowa transfer Teagan Mallegni added 17 points, hitting six of eight shots overall and five of seven from 3-point range. The Badgers played without six players: freshman Giselle Janowski, sophomores Dorja Zaja and Alba Martin Mesa, senior Kyrah Daniels and fifth-years Kadidia Toure and Shay Bollin. Janowski, Zaja, Martin Mesa, Daniels and Toure sat out a practice Oct. 26 that was open to the media. After the exhibition, Badgers coach Robin Pingeton didn’t name names but noted that an illness recently hit the team. “We didn't realize going into the day that we were only going to have eight but just had a little sickness that popped up last night,” Pingeton said. “So different rotations, people playing different positions, but I thought they really did a good job of embracing that part of it for sure." Here are three takeaways from the contests. Plenty of teaching points for the defense Wisconsin played aggressive on the ball defense, which resulted in many of its 15 steals. The players also hit the floor and hustled for loose balls. Overall, however, the execution defensively wasn’t up to Pingeton's expectations. Eau Claire, which is learning the system of a new coach, was shooting 53% (23 of 43) through three quarters though it trailed, 78-61. The Blugolds cut and passed their way to 15 layups and 23 layup attempts. They scored 34 points in the paint. “I think part of the problem is we just thought we could be so aggressive and physical and blow things up,” Pingeton said. “(Eau Claire) did a really good job playing with pace and really nailing their screens and we'd get caught and we'd trail and then we didn't give each other notifications, we didn't switch when we needed to.” Credit UW for a much better fourth quarter. Pingeton challenged the team to hold Eau Claire to no more than 10 points and delivered. The Blugolds scored eight points, just two in the paint, and shot 21.4% (3 for 14). item.title: Brewers’ William Contreras, Pat Murphy share incredible moment after World Series win
item.description: Mark Hoffman/Milwaukee Journal Sentinel Brewers’ William Contreras, Pat Murphy share incredible moment after World Series win appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Milwaukee Brewers have done it. In the franchise’s 58th year of existence, they can finally call themselves World Series champion after taking down the Tampa Bay Rays, 4-1, in Game 5 of the 2026 edition of the Fall Classic. The Brewers waited 44 years for an opportunity to redeem themselves after losing in their first and only other World Series appearance, and as the old adage goes, patience may be bitter but its fruits are sweet. Just to show how sweet it must feel for the entire Brewers team to have finally gotten over the hump, the moment star catcher William Contreras and manager Pat Murphy shared after they closed out the Rays in Game 5 says it all . Via Enrique Rojas of ESPN: Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) William Contreras y manager Pat Murphy. Eso es todo, amigos. pic.twitter.com/jyJDeuQ9i0 — Enrique Rojas/ESPN (@Enrique_Rojas1) October 29, 2026 Contreras has experienced quite a few postseason heartbreaks with the Brewers, having been part of the team’s core since 2023. He saw Milwaukee come up short in the Wild Card round in two consecutive postseasons, and then he was there to witness his team get swept by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the 2025 NLCS. But the Brewers, despite the changes their roster have gone through year after year, have stayed the course. Contreras has been a bastion of consistency , and he has relished being the leader of this elite ballclub. He is the extension of Murphy when he’s out there calling pitches and organizing his team, and now they can call themselves champion. Meanwhile, Murphy knows how to push his team’s buttons, getting the best out of them on every single turn. It’s incredible how the Brewers didn’t necessarily expect that he’ll have to take over as manager, but after Craig Counsell left rather unceremoniously , Murphy kept this team humming and not skipping a single beat. The Brewers wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for Contreras and Murphy, and they deserve all the celebrations they’ll be doing over the next few weeks as they have immortalized themselves in MLB lore. item.title: Shane Van Gisbergen Has Changed NASCAR, But The Sport Still Needs To Prove He Can Win Anywhere
item.description: Jun 28, 2026; Sonoma, California, USA; Trackhouse Racing driver Shane Van Gisbergen (97) celebrates after winning the NASCAR Toyota / Save Mart 350 series race at Sonoma Raceway. Mandatory Credit: Stan Szeto-Imagn Images Shane van Gisbergen has already proved that his road-course talent translates to NASCAR. The next question is how quickly he can become a threat everywhere. The Trackhouse Racing driver has changed expectations for international talent entering American stock-car racing. His road-course ability is exceptional, and his presence has added another compelling storyline to the Cup Series. But NASCAR is not a road-course championship. The Oval Question Still Matters Martinsville demands a different skill set. Drivers need patience in traffic, strong braking, tire management and the ability to handle repeated contact without losing their rhythm. It is not enough to be spectacular on a circuit with right turns. SVG’s supporters can reasonably argue that his overall development has been impressive. His critics can also point out that success across the full schedule is the standard for a Cup Series contender. Both things can be true. What Would Make SVG A True Championship Threat? The next step is consistency across every type of track. Winning on road courses establishes credibility, but competing for a championship requires collecting strong results on ovals, short tracks and superspeedways, too. That is a difficult transition, even for talented drivers. Van Gisbergen has the opportunity to silence more doubters as he gains experience. But the sport should not crown him an all-around master before he proves it over a full championship campaign. The potential is obvious. The challenge is proving that potential everywhere. And that is what makes his NASCAR journey worth watching.

item.title: NASCAR’s Martinsville Playoff Race Could Get Ugly Fast, And That Is Exactly What The Sport Needs
item.description: Photo by: Jim Dedmon If you want clean air, polite racing and 37 drivers staying out of each other’s way, Martinsville might not be your favorite Sunday afternoon. Good. NASCAR heads to the paperclip this weekend for a race with championship implications and almost no room for error. Kyle Larson enters with a massive points lead, while Denny Hamlin and Christopher Bell need extraordinary weekends to stay alive. The pressure should make every restart fascinating. Martinsville Is Supposed To Be Difficult Martinsville is not a track where drivers can casually cruise through traffic. The tight corners, short straightaways and heavy braking create opportunities for contact. That is part of the appeal. Fans complain when races become processional. Then they complain when drivers get aggressive enough to change the outcome. NASCAR cannot have it both ways. Short-track racing involves risk, and playoff pressure only increases the intensity. There is a difference between deliberate wrecking and hard racing. But Martinsville has a way of putting that distinction to the test. The Championship Could Turn On One Moment Larson has the points advantage, but Martinsville still demands a complete performance. A bad pit stop, damaged car or poorly timed incident could change the weekend. For the drivers chasing him, playing it safe may not be enough. That creates the kind of tension NASCAR needs during the championship fight. The sport should want drivers fighting for every position, not protecting themselves from criticism. If Martinsville delivers a wild finish, expect complaints. Also expect everyone to watch. Sometimes the best NASCAR races are the ones that leave the garage arguing long after the checkered flag.

item.title: Brewers set World Series celebration for Friday, October 30
item.description: MILWAUKEE, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 22: World Series signage is seen during a workout day prior to game on of the 2026 World Series between the Tampa Bay Rays and the Milwaukee Brewers at American Family Field on October 22, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images After capturing the franchise’s first World Series title on Wednesday night in Tampa Bay, the Milwaukee Brewers are set to return to Milwaukee to celebrate with the city and state at a parade on Friday, October 30. The championship marked the culmination of a historic season that featured the team’s first appearance in the World Series since 1982. It featured packed watch parties and sold-out crowds with unforgettable moments along the way. Brewers fans across Wisconsin and beyond helped fuel the most memorable chapter in franchise history. Together, players, coaches, staff, alumni, and fans have brought a World Series championship home to Milwaukee. The Milwaukee Brewers Championship Celebration will feature a parade through the heart of the city on historic Wisconsin Avenue, as well as a rally and fan festival to bring the community together to honor the World Series champions. The parade is set to begin at 10 a.m. at the intersection of North 4th Street and West Wisconsin Avenue, proceeding through downtown Milwaukee before concluding at Henry Maier Festival Park, where a rally will take place throughout the grounds. Admission to the festival grounds will be free to all fans until capacity is reached. Tickets for the American Family Insurance Amphitheater for the rally speeches will be available on Thursday, October 29 with staggered season seat member presales starting at 10 a.m. and public tickets on sale at 2 p.m. Net proceeds will benefit the Brewers Community Foundation. For fans without tickets, the rally speeches will be available on various video boards throughout the festival grounds. The grounds will open to the public at 8 a.m. to accommodate fans. On the grounds, guests can enjoy multiple viewing locations with large video screens featuring live parade coverage, along with live music and a variety of food and beverage offerings. For festival park entry and venue policies, visit AmFamAmp.com . Fans will also have the opportunity to purchase exclusive Brewers parade/rally merchandise during the celebration at Henry Maier Festival Park. The first 50,000 fans at the rally will also receive a limited-edition championship rally towel. The Brewers Team Store at American Family Field will open at 9 a.m. on Thursday, October 29, and will operate exclusively out of the merchandise tent located in the 3rd base plaza. To learn more about the celebration, fans should visit brewers.com/parade and follow the Brewers’ official social media channels for any additional updates.

item.title: Denny Hamlin Is Running Out Of Excuses, And Martinsville Could Decide His NASCAR Legacy
item.description: Oct 25, 2025; Martinsville, Virginia, USA; NASCAR Cup Series driver Denny Hamlin (11) before NASCAR Cup Series Xfinity 500 Qualifying at Martinsville Speedway. Mandatory Credit: Greg Atkins-Imagn Images Denny Hamlin has spent years being one of NASCAR’s best drivers without winning the Cup Series championship. Now, his latest title opportunity is hanging by a thread. Hamlin trails Kyle Larson by 73 points entering Martinsville. He needs an enormous weekend to keep his championship hopes alive. For a driver with Hamlin’s experience and equipment, that is a brutal position. The Window Is Closing Hamlin has the talent to win races. He has the team, the experience and the short-track credentials to make a serious run at Martinsville. But his 2026 postseason has been plagued by problems. Incidents, bad finishes and missed opportunities have left him chasing Larson instead of controlling the championship. At some point, the excuses stop mattering. Championships are not awarded for having a fast car or being competitive for most of the year. Drivers have to deliver when the stakes are highest. Can Hamlin Finally Change The Narrative? Martinsville gives Hamlin an opportunity to fight back. It is also a reminder of how difficult his championship mission has become. If Larson outscores him by three or more points Sunday, Hamlin’s title hopes are over. That leaves little room for another mistake. Hamlin has accomplished plenty in NASCAR, and a championship would not erase the success he has already enjoyed. But the missing title remains the obvious question surrounding his career. Is this finally the year he gets it done, or will NASCAR fans spend another offseason debating what might have been? Sunday could provide the answer.

item.title: Sophie Cunningham gives Caitlin Clark reason Indiana went from WNBA ‘nap town’ to people’s ‘Super Bowl’
item.description: Photo by Tara Walton/Getty Images In a recent podcast appearance talking to Theo Von, Sophie Cunningham explained how much the Indiana Fever’s status has changed in recent years. The Indiana Fever have been the WNBA’s most-watched franchise since they drafted Caitlin Clark. Their fame went to another level this season, even as Sophie Cunningham emerged as one of the league’s most popular figures. The team wasn’t able to go deep in the playoffs, but they remain quite loved. This wasn’t always the case. The Fever won a championship in 2012 and were decently successful in the Tamika Catchings era, but they struggled a lot after 2016. The two years before drafting Clark were arguably the franchise’s worst, and Cunningham recently noted the change she herself has witnessed. Sophie Cunningham admits Indiana Fever’s support and popularity increased dramatically during her own career Cunningham was drafted by the Phoenix Mercury in 2019 and has been in the WNBA since. The 30-year-old has been in Indiana since 2025, although there has been a lot of speculation on whether she will remain with the team moving forward. In any case, she spoke on a recent podcast about how much things have changed for the franchise since the arrival of Caitlin Clark and the other superstars from her draft class. “When I got drafted, Indiana, I think they only had like 200 fans,” Cunningham said. “Like, it was a nap town. People went there to catch up on sleep. You played a game and you wanted to get out. Now, that’s the place you want to play. That’s like people’s Super Bowl… Now, every arena’s like that.” The 2024 WNBA draft changed a lot of things around the league. Their popularity is now at an all-time high, especially the Fever. While they still do have a lot of growing to do, the past couple of years have been immense for women’s basketball overall. item.title: NASCAR Fans Better Appreciate Kyle Larson Now, Because Another Championship Could Make This Era Look Ridiculous
item.description: Sep 2, 2026; Charlotte, NC, USA; Kyle Larson answers questions from the media during the Chase media day at the Charlotte Convention Center. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images Kyle Larson is approaching a milestone that should make every NASCAR fan pay attention. The defending Cup Series champion enters Martinsville with a 73-point advantage over Denny Hamlin. He can clinch another championship this weekend. If he does, Larson will have won back-to-back titles and three championships overall. And somehow, people still argue about whether he gets enough credit. The Numbers Are Getting Hard To Ignore Larson’s 2026 season was not perfect. He endured a lengthy winless stretch before finding his form during the Chase. But that is precisely what makes his current position impressive. He recovered, won multiple postseason races and built a commanding championship lead. Now he heads to Martinsville with a chance to finish the job before the season finale. Where Does Larson Rank Among NASCAR’s Best? This is where the argument gets interesting. Larson’s raw talent has rarely been questioned. His ability to compete across different forms of racing makes him one of the most versatile drivers of his generation. But championships are what separate great seasons from great careers. If Larson clinches Sunday, the conversation about his historical standing becomes harder to avoid. If he falls short, the debate continues. Either way, NASCAR fans should enjoy watching one of the sport’s most gifted drivers build his legacy. The question is no longer whether Larson belongs among the best drivers of his era. It is how high he can climb.

item.title: Yankees Important 2026-2027 Offseason Dates
item.description: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 07: Manager Aaron Boone #17 of the New York Yankees shakes hands with his players before game three of the American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays at Yankee Stadium on October 07, 2026 in the Bronx borough of New York City. (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Yankees have long since been eliminated, and now the World Series is at an end as well. The Rays found the Brewers to be a far tougher opponent than New York or Cleveland, and the Brew Crew have captured their first championship in franchise history. Now, the MLB offseason will commence, and there are several dates to keep an eye on in the months ahead. With the lockout becoming more likely to begin in December, expect to witness a lot of cancellations, alterations, or postponements of important events such as the Winter Meetings, owner meetings, and the draft lottery. If the MLBPA and the owners’ dispute lasts deep into 2027, there’s at least a chance we may not see any baseball at all in the majors in 2027. The best-case may be something like what happened last time around, when an agreement was reached in early March and no games were ultimately lost outside of spring training; the 2022 campaign just began and ended a week later than originally planned. Regardless, the list below tracks all the important dates that you’ll need to keep track of as we make our way through the offseason, with modifications to be anticipated from the impending lockout. October 29: Free agents will automatically file at 9 a.m. EST. They won’t be allowed to sign for five days. November 1: Gold Glove Award winners will be announced at 9 p.m. EST on ESPN. item.title: The Atlanta Dream Had A WNBA Championship Within Reach And Watched It Slip Away
item.description: Aug 30, 2026; College Park, Georgia, USA; Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese (5) shoots over Minnesota Lynx forward Natasha Howard (1) during the first half at Gateway Center Arena at College Park. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images The Atlanta Dream were two wins away from a championship. Instead, they are left wondering how a promising Finals run unraveled so quickly. Atlanta took a 2-1 lead over the Golden State Valkyries after two convincing victories. Angel Reese delivered 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, while the Dream won Game 3 by 26 points. Then everything changed. Golden State won Game 4, 67-62, before closing the series with a 64-55 victory in Game 5. Atlanta managed only 117 combined points across those final two games. For a team that had championship ambitions, the finish was brutal. The Offense Disappeared When It Mattered Most The Valkyries deserve credit for adjusting defensively. They disrupted Atlanta’s rhythm, contested shots and made the Dream uncomfortable. But Atlanta also struggled to find answers. Reese scored just eight points in Game 4 and seven in Game 5. Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 19 points in Game 4, but the Dream could not generate enough offense to protect their series lead. The shooting numbers told the story. Golden State held Atlanta to 33.3% shooting in Game 4 and followed it with another defensive performance that limited the Dream to 55 points. At that point, blaming one player would miss the bigger problem. Atlanta needed multiple players to step up. It never found the consistent offensive response required to close out the series. This Was An Opportunity The Dream Cannot Take For Granted Reaching the Finals is an accomplishment. Atlanta should not lose sight of that after a painful ending. But the Dream also had a chance to win the franchise’s first championship. They held the lead in the series and had momentum after a dominant Game 3. Golden State adjusted. Atlanta did not respond well enough. That is the lesson the Dream must confront during the offseason. Championship teams need more than a strong start, a dominant star or one impressive win. They need answers when the opponent changes the game. Atlanta came close enough to see the trophy within reach. That makes the final two losses even harder to swallow. The Dream proved they could compete for a championship. Now they must prove this run was the beginning of something bigger, not their best chance gone to waste.

item.title: Angel Reese Went From WNBA Finals Hero To Biggest Question Mark In Two Games
item.description: Aug 30, 2026; College Park, Georgia, USA; Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese (5) reacts after a play against the Minnesota Lynx during the first half at Gateway Center Arena at College Park. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images Angel Reese looked like a Finals superstar. Then the Golden State Valkyries found an answer, and Atlanta’s championship hopes took a painful turn. The Atlanta Dream lost 64-55 to Golden State in Game 5 on Monday, ending their title hopes after a series that once looked firmly within reach. Reese had opened the Finals with consecutive dominant performances, including 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2. But the final two games told a different story. Reese scored eight points on 2-of-12 shooting in Game 4, then finished Game 5 with seven points and 15 rebounds. She also committed six turnovers in Game 4 and three in Game 5. Golden State Found The Blueprint The Valkyries made life increasingly difficult for Reese around the basket. Their physical defense disrupted Atlanta’s offensive rhythm and forced the Dream to work for nearly every good look. Reese still contributed on the glass. Her 15 rebounds in Game 5 demonstrated that her impact did not disappear entirely. But rebounding alone could not solve Atlanta’s offensive problems. The Dream scored just 55 points in the decisive game, struggling to generate consistent offense when the stakes were highest. That is the uncomfortable reality of a championship series. Opponents adjust, weaknesses become targets and stars must find ways to respond. The Debate Around Reese Just Got Louder Reese deserves credit for helping Atlanta reach the Finals. Her performances earlier in the series showed why she can be such a difficult matchup. But the final two games will invite uncomfortable questions about her offensive development. Can she remain effective when opponents take away her preferred looks? Can she make defenses pay when the paint becomes crowded? Those are fair basketball questions, not personal attacks. One difficult finish does not define a player’s career. Still, championship opportunities are rare, and Atlanta had a genuine chance to win the title. Reese helped get the Dream there. Now the next step is proving she can help finish the job when defenses have a full series to figure her out.

item.title: Brewers catcher Contreras named World Series MVP
item.description: William Contreras of the Milwaukee Brewers poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after the Brewers' title-clinching win over the Tampa Bay Rays (ELSA) Milwaukee's veteran catcher William Contreras was named World Series Most Valuable Player on Wednesday after excelling at the plate and behind it in the Brewers' triumph over the Tampa Bay Rays. Contreras, who became the third Venezuelan to earn World Series MVP honors, hit .382 with four runs-batted-in as the Brewers beat the Rays four games to one in Major League Baseball's best-of-seven championship series. That included a run-scoring double in the sixth inning of the Brewers' 4-1 game-five victory, which clinched the first World Series title in Milwaukee's history. The 28-year-old also caught four Rays stealing, two of them in game one. He confidently shepherded a Brewers pitching staff that stifled the Rays lineup and showed a mastery of the Automated Ball-Strike Challenge System. "I'm very proud. I don't even know what to say," an emotional Contreras said as he received the award. "I have no words to describe what I feel. I just want to thank my teammates. I love this game." The player nicknamed "Wild Bill" established himself as a Major League star 10 years after his elder brother, Willson Contreras, earned a World Series title with the Chicago Cubs. "My brother is my best friend," said Contreras, who shared an embrace with Willson moments after he was named MVP. He joined Pablo Sandoval and Salvador Perez as the third Venezuelan to earn MVP honors. Sandoval did it with the San Francisco Giants in 2012 and Perez with the Kansas City Royals in 2015. He celebrated the championship alongside Brewers teammate Jackson Chourio after the two teamed to help Venezuela win its first World Baseball Classic with a final victory over the United States in March. bb/amz

Paige Spiranac’s social media success raises an uncomfortable question: Has the sport made itself harder to discover than it needs to be? Spiranac reaches audiences through a style of content that looks nothing like a traditional golf broadcast. Her popularity illustrates how personality-driven coverage can bring the sport into conversations that might otherwise never involve a golf course. That is worth noticing, whether traditional golf media likes it or not. The Problem Is Not Golf. It Is How Golf Gets Presented. The sport has plenty of compelling stories. Rivalries, pressure-packed finishes, equipment debates and the difficulty of playing at the highest level should all make for engaging content. But a casual viewer may not know where to start. A tournament leaderboard can feel distant to someone who does not recognize the players or understand what makes a particular round important. Creators can bridge that gap by making golf feel accessible before asking people to invest hours in a tournament. Spiranac has built a recognizable platform by understanding the internet’s appetite for personality-driven content. Traditional Golf Media Should Not Ignore The Lesson This is not an argument that social media personalities are more important than professional golfers. The athletes remain the center of the competition. It is an argument that attracting attention is its own skill. Golf can protect its traditions while finding better ways to reach casual fans. Short videos, accessible explanations and recognizable personalities can help introduce new audiences to the game. Spiranac’s success offers a reminder that people do not always discover sports through the sports themselves. Sometimes they discover them through the people who make them interesting. Golf should treat that as an opportunity, not a threat.

Mandatory Credit: Brett Davis-Imagn Images Angel Reese seems to face a new set of expectations every time she steps on a basketball court. For some critics, the standard never stops changing. When Reese rebounds, the conversation can shift to scoring. When she scores, the discussion can turn to efficiency. When she speaks confidently, the debate can become about personality instead of basketball. At some point, fans have to ask whether they are evaluating a player or simply reacting to a celebrity. Criticism Is Fair. Changing The Standard Is Not. Reese is not above criticism. No professional athlete is, and her performances should be judged honestly. But meaningful analysis requires consistent standards. A player should not be praised for one skill one day and dismissed for that same skill the next. Reese’s rebounding, offensive development and overall impact are all legitimate subjects for discussion. So is how her game compares with other top players in the league. The conversation gets weaker when every performance becomes an excuse to recycle the same argument. The Debate Says Something About The WNBA Reese’s popularity means her performances attract viewers who might not otherwise follow the league closely. That attention creates opportunities, even when the conversation becomes unnecessarily personal. The WNBA needs stars who generate interest. It also needs coverage that can distinguish a rough game from a larger career judgment. Fans do not have to agree about Reese. They should at least be able to agree on what they are evaluating. If every game becomes another referendum on her entire existence as a basketball player, the analysis has probably gone too far.

item.description: The Cincinnati Bengals have made their team hall of fame more exclusive. Any hall of fame should be exclusive and set a high bar to gain membership, and the Bengals are falling more in line with how some of the elite organizations in the AFC induct former players and major team contributors into their version of Cincinnati’s Ring of Honor. But some Bengals fans and former players remain upset about the club’s decision to drop to one ROH inductee per year beginning in 2027. They want to know why, especially since the Bengals didn’t launch their Ring of Honor until 2021 after years of fans pleading for them to join the modern NFL and follow most franchises in officially recognizing past players and other significant club contributors. ROH member Willie Anderson took to social media in July and implored the Bengals to continue to induct multiple members each year. Fans and former players believe the Bengals need to continue to play catch-up by inducting multiple people each year. The Bengals, however, aren’t directly answering questions about their decision ahead of James Brooks and the late Bob Trumpy going into the Ring of Honor at halftime of the Nov. 1 game against the Tennessee Titans at Paycor Stadium. The Bengals declined to make executive Elizabeth Blackburn available to answer questions when I reached out. Blackburn oversees the ROH. Instead, I was sent links to press releases on the Bengals’ official website from May, when the announcement was made that changes were coming for the ROH. The Bengals have a right to do as they please with their ROH. They’ve come a long way in being more fan-friendly and officially acknowledging their history after decades of publicly showing they didn’t seem to care. They let season ticket holders vote on the ROH nominees each season, a great decision that will continue, a club official said. It'd still be good to offer fans a full explanation about why the change was made and why now. The memories of Robin Yount, Paul Molitor and that unforgettable team became something older fans passed down to younger generations.
